Lecture 35

Conformal maps for boundary value problems

We prove that analytic maps carry harmonic functions to harmonic functions, Dirichlet data to Dirichlet data, and normal derivatives with the factor ∣f′∣\abs{f'}∣f′∣. We prove that bounded solutions on a half-plane are determined by their boundary data, and solve problems in wedges by mapping them onto the half-plane.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Check that a given analytic function maps a region one-to-one onto another, with the boundary pieces matched, and choose the branch it needs.
  • Transport a Dirichlet problem through a conformal map and transform the solution back, and carry Neumann data with the scale factor ∣f′∣\abs{f'}∣f′∣.
  • Solve a Dirichlet problem with piecewise constant data on a half-plane or a wedge, and state the class of bounded solutions in which it is unique.
  • Recover the field from the mapped complex potential and describe its behaviour at a corner of the region.

Lecture 33 solved Laplace’s equation on a rectangle, and Lecture 34 read fields and flows from analytic functions. Many plane regions are neither rectangles nor regions on which a potential can be guessed. In this lecture we map such a region onto a simpler one by an analytic function, solve the problem there, and carry the solution back. The lecture reads in three stages: conformal maps and what they carry (Sections 35.1–35.2), the half-plane and its uniqueness theorem (Section 35.3), and wedges and corners (Sections 35.4–35.5).

35.1 Conformal maps

Throughout the lecture UUU and VVV are open subsets of the plane, identified with C\CC, and z=x+iyz=x+\iu yz=x+iy. In polar form z=reiθz=r\ee^{\iu\theta}z=reiθ.

Definition 35.1 (Conformal map). A conformal map of UUU onto VVV is a bijection f:U→Vf:U\to Vf:U→V such that fff is analytic on UUU and its inverse f−1f^{-1}f−1 is analytic on VVV.

We write w=f(z)w=f(z)w=f(z) for the image point, as in Lecture 15. The definition asks for more than analyticity. An analytic function such as z2z^2z2 on the punctured plane takes every nonzero value twice, and it has no inverse there. Each map below is therefore given together with the region on which it is one-to-one and the region it covers.

Lecture 15 showed that an analytic function with f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0 preserves the angles between curves through z0z_0z0​, and called a map with this property conformal at z0z_0z0​. The next proposition proves this again and shows that a conformal map of UUU onto VVV is conformal at every point of UUU. The converse fails. The function z2z^2z2 is conformal at every point of the punctured plane, but it is not one-to-one there. At a zero of f′f'f′ angles need not be preserved. For example, z2z^2z2 doubles the angles between curves through 000 (Lecture 15).

Proposition 35.2 (Derivative and angles). Let fff be analytic on an open set containing z0z_0z0​, with f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0. Then two curves through z0z_0z0​ with nonzero velocities cross at the same angle, and in the same sense of rotation, as their images through f(z0)f(z_0)f(z0​). If fff is a conformal map of UUU onto VVV, then f′(z)≠0f'(z)\ne0f′(z)=0 for every z∈Uz\in Uz∈U.

Proof. First, the angles. Let z1z_1z1​ and z2z_2z2​ be curves with z1(0)=z2(0)=z0z_1(0)=z_2(0)=z_0z1​(0)=z2​(0)=z0​ and nonzero velocities z1′(0)z_1'(0)z1′​(0) and z2′(0)z_2'(0)z2′​(0). By Lecture 15’s proposition on the derivative along a curve, the image curves have the velocities f′(z0)z1′(0)f'(z_0)z_1'(0)f′(z0​)z1′​(0) and f′(z0)z2′(0)f'(z_0)z_2'(0)f′(z0​)z2′​(0). The angle from the first velocity to the second is an argument of the quotient z2′(0)/z1′(0)z_2'(0)/z_1'(0)z2′​(0)/z1′​(0). The quotient of the image velocities is the same number, because the factor f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0 cancels. So the angle and its sense are the same.

Next, the derivative. If fff is a conformal map, then f−1(f(z))=zf^{-1}(f(z))=zf−1(f(z))=z on UUU. By the chain rule for analytic functions (Lecture 15), (f−1)′(f(z)) f′(z)=1(f^{-1})'(f(z))\,f'(z)=1(f−1)′(f(z))f′(z)=1, so f′(z)≠0f'(z)\ne0f′(z)=0. ■

An analytic map with f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0 rotates every velocity of a curve through z0z_0z0​ by an argument of f′(z0)f'(z_0)f′(z0​) and stretches it by the factor ∣f′(z0)∣\abs{f'(z_0)}∣f′(z0​)∣. Small figures keep their shape, while their size and orientation change from point to point.

35.2 What a conformal map carries

Let fff be a conformal map of UUU onto VVV, and let hhh be a function on VVV. The function h∘fh\circ fh∘f on UUU takes at zzz the value that hhh takes at the image point f(z)f(z)f(z). We now compare the Laplacians, the boundary values and the normal derivatives of hhh and h∘fh\circ fh∘f. We write the real and imaginary parts of the map as f=X+iYf=X+\iu Yf=X+iY, so that h∘f(x,y)=h(X(x,y),Y(x,y))h\circ f(x,y)=h(X(x,y),Y(x,y))h∘f(x,y)=h(X(x,y),Y(x,y)). By Lecture 17’s proposition that analytic functions are infinitely differentiable, XXX and YYY have continuous partial derivatives of every order. They satisfy the Cauchy–Riemann equations Xx=YyX_x=Y_yXx​=Yy​ and Xy=−YxX_y=-Y_xXy​=−Yx​, and ∣f′∣2=Xx2+Yx2\abs{f'}^2=X_x^2+Y_x^2∣f′∣2=Xx2​+Yx2​ (Lecture 15).

35.3 The half-plane

Most of our maps end on the half-plane H\mathbb HH, so we solve Dirichlet problems there. The half-plane is unbounded, and the maximum principle of Lecture 33 was proved for a rectangle. Uniqueness fails without a condition at infinity. The function u=Im⁡w=yu=\Im w=yu=Imw=y is harmonic on H\mathbb HH, continuous on the closed half-plane, and zero on the real axis, but it is not zero. A second solution of the same problem is u=0u=0u=0. The class in which uniqueness holds is that of bounded solutions, and it allows finitely many points where the data jump.

We first extend the maximum principle to the regions we need. A continuous function on a finite union of closed boxes attains a largest value there, by Lecture 29’s lemma on continuous functions on closed boxes applied to each box.

Lemma 35.7 (Maximum principle on unions of boxes). Let UUU be a bounded open set in the plane whose closure U‾\overline UU is a finite union of closed boxes and whose boundary ∂U\partial U∂U is a finite union of closed segments. Let uuu be harmonic on UUU and continuous on U‾\overline UU. Then max⁡U‾u=max⁡∂Uu\max_{\overline U}u=\max_{\partial U}umaxU​u=max∂U​u.

Proof. The proof of Lecture 33’s maximum principle applies with U‾\overline UU in place of the rectangle. The maxima of uuu and of v=u+ε(x2+y2)v=u+\varepsilon(x^2+y^2)v=u+ε(x2+y2) over U‾\overline UU and over ∂U\partial U∂U exist, because Lecture 29’s lemma gives a largest value on each of the finitely many boxes and segments. A point of U‾\overline UU that is not in ∂U\partial U∂U lies in UUU, where vvv has no maximum, by the second-derivative argument of Lecture 33, since ∇2v=4ε>0\laplacian v=4\varepsilon>0∇2v=4ε>0. With rmax⁡2r_{\max}^2rmax2​ the largest value of x2+y2x^2+y^2x2+y2 on U‾\overline UU, we get u≤max⁡∂Uu+εrmax⁡2u\le\max_{\partial U}u+\varepsilon r_{\max}^2u≤max∂U​u+εrmax2​ on U‾\overline UU and let ε→0+\varepsilon\to0^+ε→0+. ■

The theorem is the uniqueness statement for the bounded Dirichlet problem on H\mathbb HH. Two bounded harmonic functions that are continuous on the closed half-plane except at the same finitely many points and agree on the rest of the real axis are equal, because their difference satisfies the hypotheses. The example u=yu=yu=y shows that boundedness cannot be dropped.

For piecewise constant data the solution can be written down. For a real number aaa and w≠aw\ne aw=a with Im⁡w≥0\Im w\ge0Imw≥0, let ϑa(w)∈[0,π]\vartheta_a(w)\in[0,\pi]ϑa​(w)∈[0,π] be the angle of w−aw-aw−a: ϑa(w)=arccos⁡x−a∣w−a∣.\vartheta_a(w)=\arccos\frac{x-a}{\abs{w-a}} .ϑa​(w)=arccos∣w−a∣x−a​. It is continuous, being a composition of continuous functions, and on H\mathbb HH it equals Arg⁡(w−a)=Im⁡Log⁡(w−a)\Arg(w-a)=\Im\Log(w-a)Arg(w−a)=ImLog(w−a), so it is harmonic there. We use the arccosine rather than Arg⁡(w−a)\Arg(w-a)Arg(w−a) because Arg⁡(w−a)\Arg(w-a)Arg(w−a) is not defined on the ray x<ax<ax<a of the real axis, which lies on the cut of Log⁡\LogLog. On the real axis ϑa\vartheta_aϑa​ is 000 for x>ax>ax>a and π\piπ for x<ax<ax<a.

35.4 Wedges and corners

We now solve problems in wedges by opening them with (35.1), solving on H\mathbb HH with (35.7), and carrying the solution back.

35.5 Choosing a map

The method of this lecture has the following steps.

  1. Find a conformal map fff of the region UUU onto a region VVV where the problem can be solved, here H\mathbb HH. Check that fff is one-to-one on UUU, that it covers VVV, and which boundary piece of UUU goes to which piece of ∂V\partial V∂V. Choose the branch of each power or logarithm so that its cut avoids UUU.

  2. Carry the data over. Dirichlet values are unchanged. Neumann data gUg_UgU​ on ∂U\partial U∂U become the data gVg_VgV​ on ∂V\partial V∂V with gV(f(z))=gU(z)/∣f′(z)∣g_V(f(z))=g_U(z)/\abs{f'(z)}gV​(f(z))=gU​(z)/∣f′(z)∣, by (35.5), at the boundary points where fff is analytic with f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0 and VVV lies on one side of the image of ∂U\partial U∂U. A source density FUF_UFU​ on UUU becomes FVF_VFV​ with FV(f(z))=FU(z)/∣f′(z)∣2F_V(f(z))=F_U(z)/\abs{f'(z)}^2FV​(f(z))=FU​(z)/∣f′(z)∣2, as after (35.2).

  3. Solve on VVV and compose with fff. Check the boundary values on UUU directly, and the class in which the solution is unique.

  4. Recover the field from (Ω∘f)′=Ω′(f) f′(\Omega\circ f)'=\Omega'(f)\,f'(Ω∘f)′=Ω′(f)f′, and look at the points where f′f'f′ vanishes or is unbounded, and where the data jump.

The wedge, the strip and the half-plane are related by the maps of Proposition 35.3. Polygons need the Schwarz–Christoffel maps, which are built from integrals of products of powers. They are not developed here. Ablowitz and Fokas (§5.6) construct them.

Summary

A conformal map carries a plane boundary-value problem to one on a simpler region, here the half-plane, where it is solved and carried back. Harmonic functions go to harmonic functions, Dirichlet data are carried by composition, and normal derivatives acquire the factor ∣f′∣\abs{f'}∣f′∣. Bounded solutions are unique on the half-plane and on wedges, and the field follows by differentiating the mapped complex potential with Lecture 34’s convention.

  • Conformal map: f:U→Vf:U\to Vf:U→V bijective, fff and f−1f^{-1}f−1 analytic. Then f′≠0f'\ne0f′=0, and angles are preserved. An analytic fff with f′(z0)≠0f'(z_0)\ne0f′(z0​)=0 preserves angles at z0z_0z0​ but need not be one-to-one.

  • Elementary maps: az+baz+baz+b on C\CC; zβz^\betazβ from WαW_\alphaWα​ onto WβαW_{\beta\alpha}Wβα​ for β>0\beta>0β>0, βα≤2π\beta\alpha\le2\piβα≤2π, with the branch L2πL_{2\pi}L2π​; L2πL_{2\pi}L2π​ from WαW_\alphaWα​ onto the strip 0<Im⁡ζ<α0<\Im\zeta<\alpha0<Imζ<α; w=zπ/αw=z^{\pi/\alpha}w=zπ/α from WαW_\alphaWα​ onto H\mathbb HH.

  • What is carried: for fff analytic, ∇2(h∘f)=∣f′∣2(∇2h)∘f\laplacian(h\circ f)=\abs{f'}^2(\laplacian h)\circ f∇2(h∘f)=∣f′∣2(∇2h)∘f. Dirichlet values pull back by composition. Normal derivatives: ∂n(h∘f)=∣f′∣ (∂n~h)∘f\partial_n(h\circ f)=\abs{f'}\,(\partial_{\tilde n}h)\circ f∂n​(h∘f)=∣f′∣(∂n~​h)∘f. Fields: (Ω∘f)′=Ω′(f) f′(\Omega\circ f)'=\Omega'(f)\,f'(Ω∘f)′=Ω′(f)f′.

  • Uniqueness of bounded solutions: a bounded harmonic function on H\mathbb HH, continuous on the closed half-plane except at finitely many real points and zero at the other real points, vanishes. The same holds on a wedge WαW_\alphaWα​ with α<2π\alpha<2\piα<2π. Without boundedness it fails on H\mathbb HH (u=Im⁡wu=\Im wu=Imw).

  • Piecewise constant data: u=dm+π−1∑j(dj−1−dj)ϑaj(w)u=d_m+\pi^{-1}\sum_j(d_{j-1}-d_j)\vartheta_{a_j}(w)u=dm​+π−1∑j​(dj−1​−dj​)ϑaj​​(w) on H\mathbb HH, with ϑa(w)\vartheta_a(w)ϑa​(w) the angle of w−aw-aw−a in [0,π][0,\pi][0,π].

For u1u_1u1​ the field vanishes at the vertex when α<π\alpha<\piα<π, is constant when α=π\alpha=\piα=π, and is unbounded when α>π\alpha>\piα>π.

The angular factors y(θ)=sin⁡(kπθ/α)y(\theta)=\sin(k\pi\theta/\alpha)y(θ)=sin(kπθ/α) of (35.10) solve −y′′=λy-y''=\lambda y−y′′=λy with y(0)=y(α)=0y(0)=y(\alpha)=0y(0)=y(α)=0 and λ=(kπ/α)2\lambda=(k\pi/\alpha)^2λ=(kπ/α)2, an eigenvalue problem of the kind that Lecture 36 studies in general, the Sturm–Liouville problems.
